summary: With some RSVP-TE optimizations, an ingress router can receive reservation messages before every downstream node has installed forwarding state. If it starts sending traffic right away, packets may be lost. This standards-track RFC defines LSP Self-Ping, where the ingress sends probe packets to itself through the path to confirm it is ready.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending a parade down a new road, you toss a ball down it to see if it comes back. If it does, the road works.

questions: what udp port does lsp self-ping use
why does rsvp-te lose traffic after resv
subtitle: A lightweight probe an ingress router sends to itself through a new MPLS path to check that every hop is ready before traffic flows.

tldr.problem: With some RSVP-TE optimizations, the ingress router can receive a RESV message before all downstream routers have installed forwarding state. If it sends traffic right away, packets can be lost.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress sends a UDP packet addressed to itself, carrying a 64-bit Session-ID, through the new LSP. If the packet comes back, forwarding state exists all the way to the egress, and the egress needs only to forward an ordinary IP datagram.
tldr.outcome: The ingress can start sending traffic with confidence, without using control-plane resources on transit or egress routers. The trade-off is that it cannot tell whether the forwarding state is correct.

today: RFC 7746 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of LSP Self-ping.

sections.title: The Race Condition in RSVP-TE
sections.content:
Ingress Label Switching Routers (LSRs) use RSVP-TE (RFC 3209) to set up MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs). The ingress computes a path and sends a PATH message toward the egress along an Explicit Route Object. When the egress receives it, it binds a label, installs forwarding state if necessary, and sends a RESV message back upstream through the same routers in reverse. Each transit router binds a label and updates its forwarding state. When the ingress receives the RESV, it installs state and can forward traffic.

RFC 3209 says a node SHOULD be prepared to forward packets with the assigned label before sending the RESV, but does not strictly require it. Some implementations let routers send RESV before installing forwarding state (see RFC 6383), which lets routers install state in parallel and speeds up LSP setup. This creates a race condition: the ingress may start forwarding before downstream routers are ready, and traffic can be lost.

LSP Self-ping lets the ingress verify that forwarding state is installed on all downstream nodes. It is a new protocol, not an extension of LSP Ping (RFC 4379), and listens on its own UDP port. It is extremely lightweight and uses no control-plane resources on transit or egress LSRs.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a path is faster if every stop prepares at the same time. But then the first stop might say go before the last stop is ready, and things get lost.

sections.title: When Self-ping Applies
sections.content:
LSP Self-ping fits when the ingress signals a point-to-point LSP, receives a RESV showing that downstream nodes have begun but not necessarily finished installing state, and needs to confirm they have finished. It also assumes that the ingress does not need to check that the state is correct (because that is very likely), that egress control-plane resources may be scarce, and that saving them matters more than checking correctness.

It is not a general-purpose MPLS OAM tool like LSP Ping or S-BFD. It cannot reliably tell whether state is correct. For example, it will not notice an LSP that terminates at the wrong node, or a router that wrongly forwards a packet without an MPLS label. It also fails when the LSP is signaled by LDP Independent Mode, or when Reverse Path Forwarding filters are enabled on links between ingress and egress.

LSP Ping uses control-plane resources on the egress, and S-BFD either does so or needs special forwarding-plane support. Self-ping needs nothing from the egress beyond the ability to forward an IP datagram. This matters during convergence events that affect a large number of LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The ball test only tells you the road is open, not that it leads to the right town. It is quick and bothers nobody at the far end.

sections.title: The Self-ping Message
sections.content:
The message is a UDP packet that carries a session ID. If the RSVP messages that set up the LSP used IPv4, the UDP datagram MUST be in an IPv4 header; if they used IPv6, in an IPv6 header. In either case:

  • The source address MAY be configurable and by default MUST be the address of the egress LSR.
  • The destination address MUST be the address of the ingress LSR.
  • TTL or hop count MAY be configurable and by default MUST be 255.
  • DSCP MAY be configurable and by default MUST be CS6 (110000).
  • The UDP source port MUST come from the dynamic range 49152-65535.
  • The UDP destination port MUST be lsp-self-ping (8503).

The UDP payload is a single 64-bit Session-ID that associates a message with a Self-ping session.
sections.plainLanguage: The ball has your own home address and a number written on it, so when it rolls back you know which throw it was.

sections.title: Self-ping Procedures
sections.content:
The ingress creates a short-lived session and keeps all state locally: the 64-bit Session-ID, a Retry Counter (maximum number of probes, set by configuration), a Retry Timer (milliseconds to wait after each probe, set by configuration) and a boolean Status that starts FALSE.

Until Status is TRUE or Retry Counter reaches zero, the ingress formats a message with the Session-ID, sends it through the LSP under test, and starts the timer. If a message for the session returns, Status becomes TRUE. Otherwise the counter is decremented and the timer may optionally be increased by a back-off algorithm.

The message is addressed to the ingress itself. If forwarding state exists on all downstream LSRs, the egress sees it is addressed to the ingress and forwards it back like any other IP packet. It may reach the egress with or without an MPLS header, depending on penultimate hop popping, and the egress removes the header if present. If the egress's most preferred route back is through an LSP it uses that LSP; otherwise it sends the packet without MPLS encapsulation. When the session ends, the result is returned to the invoking protocol, such as RSVP-TE.
sections.plainLanguage: You keep tossing the ball, waiting a bit between tosses, until it comes back or you run out of tries.

sections.title: Bidirectional LSPs
sections.content:
A bidirectional LSP has an active side that calculates the ERO and signals the forward direction, and a passive side that reverses the ERO and signals the reverse direction. With Self-ping, each side runs its own session, and neither forwards traffic until its local Self-ping returns TRUE.

The two sessions are independent and need not use the same Session-ID. Each endpoint may start forwarding as soon as its own session succeeds, without waiting for the other.
sections.plainLanguage: Two friends each test their own direction of the road. Each can start walking as soon as their own ball returns.

sections.title: Security and the Rejected Alternatives
sections.content:
Self-ping messages are easily forged, so an attacker could make the ingress end a session early. Operators SHOULD filter Self-ping packets at the edges of the MPLS signaling domain, and implementations SHOULD NOT assign Session-IDs predictably; a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator can help. IANA has assigned UDP port 8503 for MPLS LSP Self-Ping.

The appendix explains two rejected approaches. Using LSP Ping was rejected because each ingress controls its own probe rate but an egress must answer every ingress, and an MPLS Echo Request goes to the egress control plane, making the cost well above that of plain forwarding. Waiting on a fixed timer after RESV was rejected because no optimal value exists: too low does not prevent black-holing, too high slows LSP setup, and the best value depends on network-wide behavior, so it keeps changing.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could throw a fake ball back to trick you, so use secret hard-to-guess numbers. Waiting a set time was dropped because nobody can pick the right time.
